title: The Fastest Way to Fulfil a Bad Idea
author: Mutually Assured Instruction
summary: Using Robert Fitzpatrick's book The Mom Test — the idea that you shouldn't ask your mom whether your business idea is good because she'd lie to protect your feelings — the author applies this framework to the way schools evaluate and adopt new initiatives. When a leadership idea is pitched, people tend to validate rather than probe, because questioning an emotionally invested colleague feels contrarian, even when the idea hasn't been tested against the actual problem it claims to solve. The author observed Edrolo's 'Double Diamond' design process, which requires teams to first fully explore contributing factors before defining a problem, and then explore a wide range of potential solutions before converging — a contrast to the school culture of adopting the first solution that sounds plausible. The article challenges leaders and colleagues to ask for perspective rather than approval when pitching ideas, and to focus on insights about actual problems rather than validation of predetermined solutions.
points: The Mom Test principle — don't ask for validation from people who'll protect your feelings — applies directly to school initiative adoption: seeking approval rather than genuine insight fast-tracks bad ideas through organizations that can't afford them.
In schools, bad ideas often gain momentum because questioning an emotionally invested colleague feels contrarian, even when the idea hasn't been tested against the actual problem it claims to solve.

Edrolo's Double Diamond design process requires fully exploring contributing factors and defining the problem before developing solutions — a deliberate contrast to the common school pattern of adopting the first plausible-sounding solution.
When ideas are pitched without probing, organizations end up with costly, long-lived commitments to initiatives that have limited impact, but the sunk cost makes them too painful to stop.

The challenge to leaders is to fight the urge to validate whatever idea is presented and instead discuss how the problem the idea claims to solve actually impacts daily practice — seeking insight, not approval.
quotes: you wouldn’t ask your mom whether your idea is good or not because she would lie to you to protect your feelings.

Too often a bad idea will be pitched, people will validate it regardless of the impact it is likely to have and then it either dies on arrival or limps through a few years making limited to no impact.
For a school, this is the difference between fostering culture and growth and burdening staff with another exhausting add-on to their already crushing workload.
Too often we get too attached to the first solution to a problem that we don’t necessarily think about whether the idea is actually good or if there are potential knock on effects.
if you do things right the first time, you will be less likely to be launching changes which are dead on arrival.
next time you have an idea ask for perspective, not approval.
